### 2026-11-08: # AXIS — Day 1 Journal: Design Planning & Mechanical Modelling

**4h**

# AXIS — Day 1 Journal: Design Planning & Mechanical Modelling

November 6, 2026

## 1. Planning the Project

Today, I began developing Axis, an adjustable phone stand designed to provide a stable way to position a phone at different angles.

I wanted this project to be more than a basic phone holder. My goal was to create something that looked clean but also was functional. I also wanted to challenge myself in Fusion 360 by working with moving parts, screws and more mechanical connections.

After researching existing adjustable phone stands, I started developing a design that would use a pivot-based adjustment system. Instead of relying on a simple fixed support, I planned to connect the phone cradle to a mechanical support structure that would allow its angle to be changed. I wanted to follow a design like the one below, where screws are used to change the angle of the phone.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/6195d125c68da4dc8fd952a7d46afe9f26c9cf1a3ebfe7f01f5c3ef36fcc29b1.png)

## 2. Establishing the Main Features

I divided the design into different sections, each with a specific purpose.

**Adjustable Phone Cradle**

The upper section will consist of two support plates that hold the phone in position. The lower ends have small lips to stop the phone from sliding forward and the gap in the middle lets me charge the phone when its vertical, although its main use is for horizontal.

**Pivot-Based Adjustment Mechanism**

The phone cradle connects to the supporting arm through pivot joints. These joints allow the upper section to rotate while keeping a connection to the base. I designed the mechanism around multiple points to provide support and controlled movement.

**Side-Mounted Adjustment Knob**

An important part  of AXIS is the cylindrical adjustment knob on the side of the mechanism. Its textured outer surface will give it a better grip and gives the design a more mechanical appearance. The knob is intended to make angle adjustments easier.

**Supporting Linkage**

Behind the phone cradle, I have a structural assembly that connects the upper section to the base. This helps distribute supports the cradle when positioned at different angles.

**Three-Point Base**

Rather than using a solid rectangular base, I designed a raised triangular-style frame with four contact feet in each corner. This reduces the amount of material used while providing multiple support points. The enlarged feet also help distribute the load and improve stability.

For reference, I looked at how other adjustable phone designs worked.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/636a615a2a03f6776befef8a37cb7e7c5f18961a84d979976b67508a193e9f3f.png)

## 3. Breaking Down the CAD Model

Before modelling the complete assembly, I planned the individual components that would make up AXIS.

I decided to model the components separately so that I could adjust their dimensions and positions without having to rebuild the entire design.

## 4. Practising Screw and Fastener Modelling

Before moving into the more complicated parts of the assembly, I spent time practising how to create screws and threaded components in Fusion 360.

I experimented with cylindrical geometry and the built-in Thread feature, learning how to control thread diameter, pitch, and length. I also explored the Coil feature to better understand how the helical geometry is generated.

An important part of this practice was understanding how fasteners connect separate components. I experimented with cylindrical shafts and holes so that parts could be  secured together.

This was important for Axis because the pivot joints and connecting points needed to be positioned very accurately. Even small differences could affect how the components fit together.

I followed a few video tutorials to get a basic understanding of how screws work in 3d modeling.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/952f588e672dcf8a0491ab264ac9a93a123bb59214bc11a03cb385af1f87cf6f.png)

## 5. Developing the Mechanical Structure

Once I had a better understanding of each component, I began considering how the entire mechanism would fit together.

One of the main design considerations was balancing the weight of the phone. Since the cradle would extend away from the base, I needed to make sure that the supporting structure could handle the weight.

I also considered the positioning of the pivot joints. They needed to be aligned properly so that the phone cradle could rotate without interfering with the surrounding support components.

Now that I knew what components, I wanted to build, I did a quick sketch of what I wanted the stand to look like.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/8d6555e79e897a9c5f448f3b5747f2b8154677ed1559930374ee41f8f3840513.png)

## 7. End-of-Day Progress

I have established the overall design direction for Axis, identified its main components, and practised creating screws and threaded geometry in Fusion 360.

**Next steps:** Refine the dimensions of the individual components, develop the main mechanisms, and begin testing the assembled model's movement and stability.

### 2026-11-08: # AXIS — Day 2 Journal: Modelling & Completing the Design

**6h**

# AXIS — Day 2 Journal: Modelling & Completing the Design

Date: November 8+9

Today, I focused on turning my initial plans for AXIS into a complete 3D model. Yesterday was mostly spent researching existing phone stands, planning the design, and practising how to create screws and threaded components. Today, I wanted to put those skills to use by modelling every individual part of the stand.

I decided to build AXIS using separate components rather than creating the entire design as one solid object. This would make it easier to modify individual parts and organize the model. I also wanted to make sure the different components could fit together properly instead of just looking good individually.

I worked through the design one section at a time, starting with the base and gradually moving towards the phone cradle, support structure, adjustment knob, and smaller connecting pieces. There were a few issues along the way, particularly with dimensions, alignment, and some of the geometry. I ended up revisiting several sketches and making adjustments before I was happy with the result.

## 1. Modelling the Base

I started with the base because it would determine the positioning and proportions of almost everything else.

I began by creating a sketch from the top view. Using lines and arcs, I outlined the general shape of the base and adjusted its proportions until I was satisfied. Once the sketch was complete, I used the Extrude tool to give it thickness.

After establishing the main shape, I started refining the geometry. I used the Fillet tool to round off some of the sharper edges and make the base look more like a finished product. I also added the raised sections where the supporting structure would eventually connect.

**Problem 1 — The base looked too bulky**

My first version was noticeably thicker and wider than I wanted. Although it looked sturdy, it made the stand feel unnecessarily heavy and took away from the cleaner appearance I was aiming for.

I initially considered fixing this by changing the extrusion, but I realized that the proportions of the original sketch were also part of the problem. I went back and adjusted the sketch dimensions before refining the extrusion. I also cut out sections from the middle to make it lighter.

I also ran into an issue when applying fillets to some of the tighter corners. Fusion 360 wouldn't complete the operation with the radius I had selected. I reduced the radius and applied the fillets to smaller groups of edges instead.

After a few adjustments, the base looked much more balanced. It still had enough thickness to appear structurally sound without overwhelming the rest of the design.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/96beabb3a6545f79169fd0c1cb8e072b41c5be2669f64ad09bc417d80131e475.png)

For the base, you can see the holes I have in all four corners for the feet, as well as circular notches that will have bolts going through them to connect the other pieces.

## 3. Creating the Phone Cradle

Once the base was finished, I moved on to the upper section that would actually hold the phone.

I designed the cradle using two separate raised support plates rather than one completely solid platform. This gave the design a more open appearance and left room around the bottom of the phone for a charging cable.

I started with a sketch of the support plates and used extrusions to create their thickness. I then added the lower retaining lips, which are designed to prevent the phone from sliding forward when resting on the stand.

I spent some time adjusting the spacing and proportions of these supports. They needed to be wide enough to hold the phone securely, but I didn't want them to look oversized. I also wanted both sides to line up properly with one another.

**Problem 2 — The support plates weren't symmetrical**

When I first created the two support plates, I noticed that they weren't positioned perfectly evenly. I had been adjusting their locations manually, which made it difficult to keep the spacing consistent.

Instead of continuing to move them around, I returned to the original sketch and used dimensions and constraints to control their positions. This made the two supports much more consistent and prevented the same issue from happening again.

**Problem 3 — The retaining lips were too large**

My first attempt at the lower retaining lips made them stick out too far. They would have held the phone in place, but they made the cradle look more like a tray than a phone stand.

I reduced their height and adjusted their thickness so that they would still prevent the phone from sliding without taking up unnecessary space.

After refining the edges, I was happy with how the cradle looked. It was simple, but it had all the features I wanted without adding unnecessary geometry.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/0bd38518ab9be1c3e3fb3255eece8d65ef5e7749bce3598cac8e3040aaa658e7.png)

## 4. Modelling the Rear Support Structure

The next major component was the rear support structure connecting the phone cradle to the base. This was one of the more interesting parts of the design because it needed to provide support while also allowing the upper section to be adjusted.

I used a combination of rectangular and cylindrical geometry to create the supporting sections and connection points. I wanted the structure to look sturdy without making it unnecessarily thick or complicated.

I started by sketching the main support shapes and extruding them. From there, I added cylindrical sections where the different components would connect. These were particularly important because they formed the pivot connection points for the adjustable assembly.

I had to pay attention to the dimensions and positioning of these features. If the connection points were even slightly misaligned, the phone cradle would not sit properly when everything was assembled.

**Problem 4 — Misaligned pivot holes**

When I first created the cylindrical connection points, some of the holes and shafts weren't lining up correctly with their corresponding components.

I initially tried moving the features manually, but this caused additional alignment issues elsewhere in the model. I eventually went back into the sketches and used reference geometry to position the connection points more accurately.

This made the support structure much easier to work with and gave me a more reliable foundation for the rest of the assembly.

I also checked the thickness of the supporting sections. I wanted to avoid making them too thin, especially around the cylindrical connections, since those areas would experience more force than some of the other parts.

Once I was satisfied with the shape and positioning, I moved on to the adjustment knob.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/0cee06152a0fd91d2d1af8befa1b864cf35d230ac3507a1fbb35e1231ec078f3.png)

## 5. Creating the Side Adjustment Knob

The side-mounted adjustment knob was another feature I wanted to spend time refining because it is one of the most noticeable parts of AXIS.

I started with a circular sketch and used the Extrude tool to create the main cylindrical body. I then added the central connection section that would allow the knob to attach to the rest of the mechanism.

My first version was essentially just a plain cylinder. Although the shape was functional as a starting point, it looked unfinished compared to the other components.

I decided to add repeated details around the outside to create a textured gripping surface. This gave the knob a more mechanical appearance and made it look like an intentional adjustment component.

I experimented with the spacing and depth of these details until I was happy with the result. I also adjusted the overall proportions because I didn't want the knob to be too large compared to the base and supporting structure.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/0960c66d4638cc546aa993646c36370fcc6d83af6b9af86cd9004f6d2a50368f.png)

## 6. Modelling the Smaller Connecting Components

After finishing the larger sections, I moved on to the smaller mechanical pieces. These included cylindrical pins, connecting shafts, and other details needed to bring the assembly together.

Although these parts were relatively simple compared to the base and support structure, they still required careful measurements. Their dimensions needed to correspond with the holes and connection points I had already created.

I also applied some of the techniques I had practised yesterday when working with screws and threaded geometry. I experimented with cylindrical shafts and threaded features while considering how the different components would fit together.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/1e21d024953705e0ddd7c33073014ef0ddc3d6fe41401549034e837187b56901.png)

## 7. Bringing the Components Together

Once all the individual parts were modelled, I started assembling everything in Fusion 360.

This was probably the most satisfying part of the day because I could finally see the complete design taking shape.

I positioned the phone cradle above the rear support structure, aligned the cylindrical pivot connections, and connected the supporting assembly to the three-point base. I then positioned the adjustment knob on the side and checked how the smaller connecting components fitted into the design.

Seeing everything together also revealed a few issues that weren't obvious when I was modelling the components separately.

**Problem 7 — Some components were overlapping**

During my first assembly attempt, I noticed that a few of the components were intersecting slightly. Some of the cylindrical sections were also positioned too close to the surrounding support structure.

I went back through the model and adjusted the positions of the affected components. I checked the spacing and clearances between the different parts until the assembly looked properly aligned.

I also spent some time looking at the design from different angles to make sure there weren't any obvious issues with the proportions or placement of the components.

After these adjustments, I was happy with how everything came together. The stand finally looked like the product I had originally planned rather than a collection of separate CAD parts.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/9fa795152b8d6da20b7901dbf1d72abfef5cbd481ff59458e362edf6b0d71e72.png)

## 8. Final Result

By the end of today, I had finished modelling all the individual components and completed the full Axis design in Fusion 360.

The final model includes:

- A  base with 4 extended supporting feet.
- Two raised phone support plates.
- Lower retaining lips to prevent the phone from sliding.
- A rear supporting structure.
- Cylindrical pivot connections.
- A side-mounted adjustment knob with textured grip details.
- Smaller connecting pins and mechanical components.
- Space around the lower cradle for charging cable access.

I'm happy with how the final design turned out. What started as a simple idea for an adjustable phone stand became a much more involved CAD project once I started breaking it down into separate mechanical components.

The biggest challenge was making sure that everything fit together properly. It was easy to create individual shapes, but getting their dimensions, spacing, and connection points right took much more attention.

I also became more comfortable using Fusion 360's sketching, extrusion, fillet, and component organization tools. More importantly, I got a better understanding of how to approach a design that contains multiple connected parts.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/7c7b2babf34b1df9d08ae2a20bc6bcf27270cab8f6b18379c6592234ffa0ed8c.png)

## 9. What's Left — GitHub and BOM

With the CAD model complete, the actual design work for AXIS is finished. I don't have any major modelling tasks remaining, so the only things left are organizing and documenting the project.

My remaining tasks are:

1. Organize the Fusion 360 project files and export the necessary models.
2. Create a Bill of Materials (BOM) listing the components, materials, and estimated costs.
3. Set up the GitHub repository.
4. Write the README explaining Axis, its features, and the design process.

I want the GitHub repository to be organized properly so that someone looking at it can understand how the project was designed and what went into making it.

Overall, today was a major milestone. All the individual components have been modelled, the full assembly is complete, and AXIS has gone from an initial concept to a finished Fusion 360 design.

**Next up: BOM, GitHub, and final project documentation.**
